title: Maximum Cakes Held While Trading
statement:
A man leaves his house carrying `N` cakes and visits `K` places, one after another, before reaching home. At each place he does exactly one of three things:

- **buy** one cake (his count goes up by 1),
- **sell** one cake (his count goes down by 1; he can only do this if he is currently holding at least one cake),
- **do nothing**.

By the time he reaches home he must have sold **exactly `L` cakes** in total (over all the places).

Among all possible ways he can act that satisfy these rules, find the **maximum number of cakes he can be holding at any point of the journey** (the starting moment, after each place and the end all count). If there is no valid way to act, print `-1`.
inputFormat: A single line containing three integers `N`, `K` and `L`.
outputFormat: Print one integer: the maximum number of cakes held at any moment, or `-1` if the rules cannot be satisfied.

examples.explanation: Buy at the first 3 places (3 → 6 cakes), then sell at the last 2 places (6 → 4). He sells exactly 2 cakes, and no schedule can reach more than 3 + (5 − 2) = 6.
He starts with nothing, so to sell 2 cakes he must first buy at least 2, which needs 4 places in total, but there are only 3.
All four places must be used for selling, so he can never buy and the count only goes down from 4.

hints: Selling L cakes uses up L of the K places. What is the best use of the remaining places if you want a high peak?
If all the remaining places are buys, performed before the sells, the peak is N + (K - L). Why can no schedule do better?

That schedule is only legal if he never has to sell from an empty basket. Work out when N and the number of buys are enough to cover all L sales, and when it is impossible even with the best ordering.
